title: [Lyft Engineering] Rerouting the Stream: How Lyft Moved to the Apache Flink Kubernetes Operator
summary: Written by Maheep Myneni, Arda Kuyumcu, and Prem Santosh Udaya Shankar at Lyft.Why We Migrated: Technical Debt Meets Modern Streaming DemandsOver the past several quarters, Lyft’s Streaming Compute team retired our internally developed Flink Kubernetes operator and moved our entire streaming fleet onto the open-source Apache Flink Kubernetes operator. This post is about why we made the switch, how we pulled it off incrementally without disrupting users, and the follow-on work it took to actually get the benefits we were after.Back in 2020, when we first architected the Lyft Flink Kubernetes Operator, it was exactly what we needed. At that time, the open-source community hadn’t yet built a dedicated control plane, so we built our own to manage all streaming applications on Kubernetes. It worked well for our initial workloads, but as our real-time data needs increased and our engineers’ scope of ownership grew in both breadth and complexity, the cracks started to show.First came the maintenance burden. Our operator had become a relic of Lyft’s early Kubernetes days, kept alive by a growing pile of custom code. Every Flink version upgrade meant carefully picking through layers of accumulated technical debt and hoping nothing broke on the way through.Second came the feature gap. Streaming tooling kept moving, and our engineers kept asking for capabilities that had become table stakes elsewhere, such as autoscaling to right-size jobs, automatic rollbacks on failed deploys, and an end to hand-tuning CPU and memory. Each request left us with two options, neither of which was ideal. We could explain why we couldn’t support it yet, or spend weeks rebuilding something the open-source community had already shipped.Third was the dependency problem. We were pinned to outdated libraries. That doesn’t break anything today, but it almost always creates new issues down the line. Security patches lagged, modern Kubernetes features stayed out of reach, and every quarter we waited made the eventual escape messier.Meanwhile, the Apache Flink Kubernetes Operator had matured into production-grade infrastructure, and its feature set read like our wishlist: intelligent job-vertex autoscaling to kill backpressure, automatic memory tuning, safe upgrade mechanisms, and a robust reconciliation loop. Additionally, it was battle-tested by companies at massive scale. The decision in front of us became obvious. We needed to migrate Lyft’s fleet, hundreds of critical streaming jobs, from our internal operator to the Apache one. However, we had to do this migration without disrupting existing deployment patterns, altering our team’s workflows, or causing massive outages in production.This is the story of how we pulled it off, and why sometimes the best code you can write is the code you delete.Our Legacy: The Lyft Flink Kubernetes OperatorBefore we dive into the migration itself, it’s worth understanding what we were migrating from. The Lyft Flink Kubernetes Operator served us well for years, and being familiar with its architecture helps illustrate both why the migration was necessary and why it was nontrivial.At its core, Lyft’s operator follows the standard Kubernetes pattern by continuously watching custom resources and reconciling their state. We defined Flink applications using a FlinkApplication custom resource that looked something like this:apiVersion: flink.k8s.io/v1beta1kind: FlinkApplicationmetadata: name: my-streaming-job namespace: productionspec: image: lyft/my-flink-job:v1.2.3 flinkVersion: "1.16" jarName: "my-streaming-job.jar" entryClass: "com.lyft.streaming.MyJob" parallelism: 8 jobManagerConfig: replicas: 1 resources: memory: "2048Mi" cpu: "1.0" taskManagerConfig: taskSlots: 4 resources: memory: "4096Mi" cpu: "2.0" flinkConfig: state.backend.fs.checkpointdir: s3://lyft-flink/checkpoints state.savepoints.dir: s3://lyft-flink/savepoints execution.checkpointing.interval: 60sLyft’s operator takes this spec and creates the necessary Kubernetes resources: a JobManager (JM) deployment, a TaskManager (TM) deployment, any external runtime configurations, and optionally an ingress for the Flink UI. Simple enough, in theory.The State Machine: Where Things Got InterestingThe Lyft operator’s real complexity lived in the state machine. Deploying a stateful streaming application isn’t like deploying a stateless web service; you can’t simply kill the old pods and start new ones. If you did, all in-flight data and state would be lost. Our operator walked through a careful choreography of states to ensure zero data loss.Dual Deployment Mode (our default) had minimal, but non-zero downtime. When a user updated a FlinkApplication, the operator would spin up a completely new Flink cluster alongside the running one. Once the new cluster was healthy, it would trigger a savepoint on the old job, wait for it to complete, cancel the old job, tear down the old cluster, and finally submit the job to the new cluster from the savepoint.BlueGreen Mode took it a step further for truly zero-downtime deployments. Both clusters would run simultaneously (“dual running”), and you would manually switch traffic by setting a tearDownVersionHash field after verifying the new version was working correctly. This gave users a manual kill switch, which worked well for critical jobs where one would want to inspect the new version before committing.The state machine tracked states like ClusterStarting, Savepointing, SubmittingJob, Running, DeployFailed, and our favorite debugging companion, Recovering (for when savepoints failed and we needed to fall back to externalized checkpoints). Each transition was carefully orchestrated with retry logic, timeout handling, and event logging.Problems: The Cracks in the FoundationBeyond the maintenance burden and the feature gap, two specific pain points made this decision unavoidable. Both stemmed from early design choices that suited a smaller fleet, but broke down as our workloads grew to be more varied over time.Savepoint FragilitySavepoints were the only first-class mechanism for preserving application state during upgrades. If a savepoint failed, the operator fell back to looking for an externalized checkpoint. However, the checkpoint fallback was a last-resort recovery path rather than a strategy users could deliberately choose. The savepoint trigger had no retry logic and no idempotency guarantees. If no recent checkpoint was available, the deploy either failed or restarted the job with no state at all. For large-state jobs where savepoints were slow or occasionally timed out, a transient failure escalated into a full recovery cycle. The Apache operator introduced last-state as an explicit upgrade mode, which uses high-availability metadata or the latest checkpoint by design. This was exactly the robustness we needed, particularly for jobs where an unhealthy JobManager couldn’t cooperate with a savepoint request.Rigid Resource ModelOur operator exposed a single systemMemoryFraction knob. This represented a fraction of container memory reserved for non-JVM use. For pure Flink Java applications, this overhead was often unnecessary. For Apache Beam workloads using the Python SDK harness, it was vital. Unfortunately, how much memory those Python processes actually needed was essentially guesswork, since usage happened inside the Flink memory model. There was no observability into the utilization and no way to tune it systematically. If we set it too low, TMs would get OOM-killed. If we set it too high, we wasted resources.Migration: Our Blueprint for a Seamless SwitchSetting up a new system is the easy part. The real nightmare of any migration is unwinding everything that still points to the old one. At Lyft, all Flink deployment configs start as Jsonnet files. We use a shared module to set up operational defaults, and individual teams layer their own application configs on top:common.sp.FlinkApplication("myflinkapplication", "staging", "myproject") { application+: { spec+: { parallelism: 8, flinkConfig+: { "state.backend": "filesystem", "restart-strategy.fixed-delay.delay": "10s" } } },}In the above example, an individual app extends the base factory with its own parallelism and Flink configuration. The entire system was built around the legacy operator’s FlinkApplication custom resource definition (CRD). Rewriting every library and application overlay to natively produce the Apache operator’s FlinkDeployment CRD would have been a massive and risky undertaking.Instead, we chose to translate at the boundary, so teams could continue defining their applications exactly as they always had. The translation from FlinkApplication to FlinkDeployment happens within our deploy API. When the deploy API encounters a legacy resource, it converts the resource into something the Apache operator is familiar with. This handles the structural mapping:Job Spec: We assemble flat fields like jarName and parallelism into the Apache operator’s nested spec. jarName becomes a jarURI.Upgrade Mode: We default to last-state to restore state from the last checkpoint if possible, and map legacy configs like savepointDisabled to stateless.Pod Templates: Inline container configs on the legacy spec like node selectors, tolerations, and sidecar annotations get promoted into proper PodTemplateSpec objects.Backwards Compatibility: We inject legacy environment variables like APP_NAME and HOST_NAME so application code doesn’t break.Crucially, the migration was incremental. Dynamic configuration allowed us to migrate one application at a time, starting with staging. If an app hit issues, we could instantly roll it back to the legacy operator. To the developer, the change was largely invisible.From the Trenches: Additional Work to Integrate the OperatorWhile the translation layer got us onto the Apache operator, the migration was not yet done. We still had to address a few follow-on problems, and do additional work to make sure we saw all the benefits the Apache operator had to offer. Two of those benefits are autoscaling, which dynamically adjusts a job’s parallelism, and autotuning, which adjusts the memory resources each TaskManager gets.BlueGreen DeploymentsOnce we migrated apps onto the Apache operator, every deploy cost us an average of 3–6 minutes of downtime, and closer to 20 minutes for our largest jobs. Lyft’s operator had managed JobManager and TaskManager lifecycles together through a complex graph of operations, which kept downtime to a minimum. The Apache operator took a different approach; it spun up only the JobManagers, configured them with the relevant savepoint and resource specs, and let them coordinate the TaskManagers. Each deploy walked through the full sequence of taking a savepoint, triggering the JM pods to tear down TM pods, tearing down the JM pods, and then starting the new FlinkDeployment’s JMs using the recently taken savepoint, which then brought up the new TM pods. For a real-time business like Lyft, this was unacceptable for several of our most important use cases.The fix for this was FlinkBlueGreenDeployments, a newer CRD that maintains underlying FlinkDeployment objects so a new version can come up alongside the old one before any cutover. This feature was still under development when we started testing it internally; we hit a bug in how the operator renamed Flink configuration fields under BlueGreen, and contributed a minor upstream fix. Benefiting from the open-source community’s efforts and being able to contribute back further reinforced our decision to move to an open-source solution.AutoscalingThe Apache operator’s autoscaler uses metrics like operator busyness, backpressure, and record backlog in Kafka and Kinesis to adjust each job’s parallelism. Traffic across most of Lyft’s use cases is highly variable and stream processing is expensive, so autoscaling was, in theory, an obvious win. In practice, our Flink version (v1.17) required apps to restart in order to rescale, and the apps that would benefit the most from autoscaling were precisely the ones that couldn’t afford restart-induced downtime.Upgrading to Flink v1.19 unlocked two important changes. First, it unlocked in-place autoscaling. Jobs could change parallelism without restarting, which both preserved data freshness and avoided the spiky catch-up traffic we used to see when jobs resumed from offsets that were a few minutes old. Second, it enabled an upgrade to the new Amazon Kinesis Source Connector, which emits record backlog metrics for Kinesis streams the same way the Kafka source does. This gave the autoscaler the signal it needed to make scaling decisions on Kinesis-bound jobs, which had previously been a blind spot.AutotuningAutotuning appealed to us for two main reasons. It promised dynamic right-sizing to cut cloud costs, and it spared our devs from tuning resource configurations by hand. However, we ran into an unexpected problem after we rolled this feature out.Our Apache Beam workloads run user code in a Python SDK harness, which lives outside the Flink memory model. The Apache operator didn’t register that we were reserving memory for those Python processes inside the JVM overhead allocation. We had been tucking it there for years because most of our jobs barely touched their JVM overhead anyway. This hack worked until we enabled autotuning. The operator saw that these memory pools were not really used by Flink, and reclaimed them, OOM-killing TaskManagers across our Beam fleet. We ultimately moved the Python harness out of the Flink container entirely, running it as a sidecar in the same pod with its own resource limits.Another awkward property of autotuning is that it doesn’t play well with in-place autoscaling. To tune a job’s resources, the operator has to restart it. We weren’t willing to give up either feature, so we settled on a two-tier approach where business-critical applications that power pricing, routing, and similar real-time decisions disable autotuning and keep in-place autoscaling. Less critical applications that could tolerate some downtime use both autotuning and autoscaling with restarts.KarpenterThese features also made our node infrastructure obsolete. Before autotuning, we bin-packed pods onto AWS nodes efficiently by enforcing 1:4 or 1:8 CPU:memory ratios with power-of-two values. Autotuning broke this. The same application could have very different ratios from one tuning cycle to the next, and a static node pool could not keep up. We adopted Karpenter, which provisions EC2 nodes on demand based on what each pod actually needs, optimizing for cost or utilization as appropriate.This two-tier autotuning model produced an additional unexpected efficiency win related to unused spend (the share of compute resources we are paying for that ends up unallocated). If we are paying for an 8-core node with 32GB of memory, but only allocate 4 cores and 16GB, half of the cost of the node is unused. We had already deployed a custom Kubernetes pod scheduler on our EKS cluster that uses a “most-allocated” strategy, packing pods onto busy nodes first. When autoscaling restarted apps to rescale them, the pods had a chance to move from under-allocated nodes to densely packed ones, letting us shed underutilized nodes.ConclusionThis migration was a multi-quarter journey that often felt like changing the engines on a plane mid-flight. It took longer than expected to completely sunset our in-house operator, as there was a mess of state-machine quirks, memory model mismatches, and CRDs that didn’t translate cleanly. However, the difference in the platform after completing this migration is hard to overstate; the operator maintenance that used to eat engineering time on every Flink upgrade has been minimized, and the autoscaler is doing what we had hoped, which is right-sizing a fleet that had been overprovisioned by a few million dollars per year.The important, but hard-to-quantify benefit is that we stopped being the only contributors to our operator and infrastructure. When we noticed the BlueGreen bug, we filed an issue and a fix landed upstream within days. Our team’s posture changed from “we maintain this thing” to “we use this thing, and sometimes improve it for everyone,” which is a much better place to be. What’s next is the work we actually wanted to focus on from the start. We’re building faster feedback loops for marketplace pricing, handling autonomous vehicle telemetry, and scaling streaming primitives for Lyft’s next chapter. The Apache operator finally gave us the breathing room to work on these challenging problems.AppreciationSpecial thanks to Anirudh Adkar and Ravi Magham, who provided guidance to us throughout the project, and Janice Lee, Rohan Varshney, and Yigal Kassel for their contributions to the team’s operations. The migration would not have been possible without their efforts.Finally, thanks to our many internal customers of Lyft’s Streaming Compute platform, who bore with us and provided ample helpful feedback throughout the migration, including but not limited to Kyle Bilton and Taylor Wilson.Lyft is hiring! If you love the idea of solving ambiguous problems in technology and infrastructure, visit Lyft Careers to see our openings.Rerouting the Stream: How Lyft Moved to the Apache Flink Kubernetes Operator was originally published in Lyft Engineering on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
summary: By Praneeth Yenugutala, Victor Dusa, Anastasia Samoilova, Megan Ren, Justin Wei, Marcelo MaywormAt Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines.Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.Rules work well for known patterns, but their coverage grows only when someone recognizes a new failure mode, understands the logs, writes a rule, and keeps it current as engines and log formats change. Over one three-month period, Pensive processed roughly seven million job-failure classifications, yet about half fell into the unknown bucket. We needed a way to expand coverage without giving up the deterministic parts of Pensive that already worked.To solve this ambiguous and complex problem at Netflix scale, we invested in Pensive AI to add AI-assisted error extractions and focused diagnosis and remediation guidance to our data and ML practitioners. The goal was not simply to place a model in front of a large collection of logs. We needed bounded extraction, predictable evaluation inputs, responsive product behavior, and quality checks that could follow the system from local development through production. Those requirements shaped every layer of the design, which we will discuss in this blog. Pensive AI wraps AI around deterministic processes, which gives broader coverage, low latency, controlled AI costs, and easier maintenance across the software development lifecycle. Building on this foundation, we plan to explore more agentic debugging experiences, as Part 6 describes.Early results are encouraging. AI error extraction now covers 100% of failures, including the failures that legacy Pensive classified as unknown. Failed step attempts where no one used Pensive AI averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions than attempts where someone did (an observational comparison, not a causal claim).Figure 1. Pensive AI architecture. Always-on error extraction and on-demand debugging complement each other and share log sources, the LLM gateway, tracing, and the cache. Archived logs feed offline evals and release gates.The two paths complement each other. Error extraction improves an existing capability and is always on. It lets the user of a failed Maestro workload quickly check the parts of the logs that may point to an immediate root cause. It has low latency and low cost, and it can help in a large share of cases. On-demand debugging enables a new capability. It looks at symptoms across the logs and adds the LLM’s own knowledge and reasoning for a deeper analysis, at slightly higher latency and cost. Extraction gives a fast first look at every failure, and on-demand debugging triggered by the user goes deeper when that first look is not enough.Part 1: Finding the useful errorsLegacy Pensive rules are precise, but each one captures a particular log shape. A simplified rule looks like this:- name: SparkContainerOOMlogSource: GENIE_STDERRrestartable: falseregex: "Container.*is running beyond physical memory limits.*Killing container"summary: Spark AM container runs out of memoryWith Pensive AI, we wanted to find useful errors that had no corresponding rule and adapt more easily when familiar errors changed shape after a platform upgrade. Data Portal (our UI for data pipelines) surfaces these extracted errors when available and links back to the source logs, giving practitioners a focused starting point for triage. That raises a question: how can we ask a model to identify an error without asking it to repeat a long stack trace token by token?Producing output tokens is much slower than reading input tokens. A direct transcription approach would make long errors expensive and slow. Instead, Pensive numbers the lines of each log and gives the model a sequence of {lineNumber, text} records. The model identifies the first and last lines of the error span, and Pensive reconstructs the selected text from its own log copy, leading to lower cost and better latency. This way, the model always returns two integers (start and end line number), whether the selected logs span a few lines or hundreds of lines. The displayed content comes directly from the original log, reducing hallucinations. The model can still choose the wrong range, which is why extraction quality remains an integral measurement for our AI evals, as we will discuss later.For orchestrated workflows, “Pensive AI Error Extraction” runs automatically whenever a step fails. A step attempt is one execution of a step within a Maestro workflow. Maestro already calls Pensive for a regex-derived error and restartability classification, so AI extraction runs in the same request and returns its results alongside the established fields. The overall Pensive response must return within Maestro’s hard 90-second post-processing timeout for a failed step attempt.Figure 2. Error extraction. Legacy rules always run. The AI call is bound by a shared deadline, and late calls are excluded. Pensive merges both results into one response and caches it.That deadline shaped the extraction path. Pensive extracts errors from the logs in parallel to reduce latency, and the per-log calls share one deadline set well inside Maestro’s timeout limit. A per-log extraction call that misses the deadline is excluded from the result, allowing the overall request to return on time.The data contract between Pensive AI and the various consumers needed the same care. The legacy data model contained one flattened error string; AI extraction instead returns a list of errors, one for each log source, with deep links back to the originating logs. Changing the old field in place would have broken existing clients. We introduced the new data model beside the legacy non-AI error extraction data model and continued producing both. Data Portal, our user interface for monitoring and observing data pipelines, preferred AI errors when available and fell back to the legacy value when they were not during the rollout. That allowed a gradual rollout and ensured that historical failures still display an error, since we chose not to backfill the old data due to log retention issues.The migration is still in progress today. The Data Portal UI surface used for failed Maestro steps reads the new AI extracted error field today, while the query editor (for editing and running SQL), Workbench notebooks (managed compute platform and UI to edit and run jupyter based notebooks) and some slack clients calling Pensive still use the legacy error extraction path. Each client needs a compatible schema change before it can consume the new data. Keeping both fields populated lets teams adopt the new behavior at their own pace without forcing a coordinated cutover as we continue evolving Pensive AI.Part 2: Full failure diagnosis and the product experienceBeyond error extraction, we built Pensive AI Debugging, a tool that analyzes failed step attempts and provides root-cause analysis and suggested remediations. It is available through programmatic APIs, MCP, and the product UI (Data Portal), all backed by a common entry point across the Netflix Data Platform. This shared model supports consistent behavior and custom product experiences.This diagnosis still has to arrive quickly and remain consistent across investigations. A debugging response can take tens of seconds or a minute to generate, compared with a few seconds for error extraction. We run full AI-based debugging on demand instead of automatically, which keeps costs under control because most failed steps are never opened. We treat the failed step attempt, not the person who triggered it, as the unit of work, so everyone investigating the same failed attempt sees the same diagnosis.That choice gives us a stable unit of work for caching. We cache each debugging response by step attempt. A second request becomes a key-value read instead of another AI inference call. The cache also prevents duplicate work, reducing latency and lowering costs further. This also means that a debugging generated in the Data Portal is cached and immediately retrieved for the MCP path instead of incurring another AI inference call. A conditional write creates an in-progress record, one caller starts generation, and other callers wait for the shared result to avoid conflicts when concurrent requests come in for the same step attempt failure. If generation remains in progress past an abandonment timeout, Pensive treats the record as abandoned and reclaims it. Completed responses expire after 90 days to help control costs and optimize storage because debugging requests for much older workloads are uncommon.Pensive AI supports multiple ways to initiate debugging responses. A caller can (1) read a cached response, (2) generate one if no cache entry exists, or (3) regenerate and overwrite an existing response. Those semantics support the product UI, programmatic access, and the evaluation harness while keeping the response associated with a single immutable workload failure.Figure 3. On-demand debugging. Three client actions share one entry point. A conditional write claims the step attempt. A cache hit returns the cached result. A won claim generates and streams a response, and the result persists even if the client disconnects.For users, the most important behavior is that a long-running answer feels alive. Pensive streams the response as it is produced. The service emits server-sent events, and the GraphQL layer republishes them as a WebSocket subscription for the Data Portal client.Each event carries the complete response generated so far. That duplicates a small amount of text, but it keeps the client simple: it does not need a replay buffer or token reassembly logic, and the next event corrects the display after a dropped or late event. Generation is independent of the connection that requested it. A disconnect does not cancel the work, and the final answer still reaches the cache. A hard reload can show a loading state and poll for the completed result. Within the single-page application backing the Data Portal UI, active streams are maintained independently of view and component lifecycle, so navigation does not interrupt a response in progress.Part 3: Measuring and improving the behavior we wantLLM-assisted systems need more than a demo or a few working examples. Before shipping in production, we need confidence in both error extraction and debugging guidance, and we need to know that we have not regressed on failures that legacy Pensive already handled. We built separate evaluation frameworks focused on the two distinct jobs.Building labeled data is often the expensive part of evaluation. For error extraction, legacy Pensive’s hand-written rules provide reference labels for failures they recognize. They also serve as excellent ground truth in most cases. We run those rules over production logs and compare their extracted spans with Pensive AI’s output. This gives us a reliable regression set without relabeling every example by hand, though it is not an absolute ground truth (since our human-built rules could also have been stale). For now, we keep these rules frozen as a label source. This lets us continue to build comparison evals and run them on top of the existing system.Stable inputs are essential for repeatable evaluation experiments where we A/B test new models/configurations or context injections to improve response quality. The logs Pensive AI uses can expire after as few as seven days or as many as 30 days. Production Pensive AI requests archive fetched logs to S3 object storage asynchronously during workload execution time so the upload is not on the user-facing critical path. Uploads do not overwrite an existing object, preserving the exact snapshot used to create an evaluation case. Evals use those archived logs, so score changes remain attributable to the system under test. The archive also prevents parallel experiments from overloading the source systems and lets us run them without affecting production. Cached S3 log inputs further reduce costs when running evaluations.Concretely, we measure four complementary signals for error extraction:Inclusion: An LLM judge compares the legacy Pensive error for a failure with the errors Pensive AI extracted and determines whether the known error is still represented, even when wording differs.Precision: A second judge sees only the extracted AI errors and evaluates whether each is meaningful and actionable on its own.Repeated noise: A script looks across the whole dataset for lines that recur too often. A generic status line may look harmless in one answer but become distracting if it appears in a large share of failures. Lines appearing in more than about 30% of workflows are candidates for explicit exclusion. In practice, the exclusion list has only three lines, each of which otherwise appeared in nearly every extracted error.Latency: We record the latency of every extraction call. Quality scores alone cannot reveal when an apparent improvement requires too much additional work, which often correlates with increased AI costs.This combination gives us an actionable feedback loop. Prompt changes can reduce general noise, while the dataset-level view exposes the stubborn boilerplate that prompt changes do not eliminate. Existing rules act as a regression floor, and archived logs give us a repeatable way to compare changes. At Pensive AI’s scale, model and system choices must satisfy quality, latency, maintainability and cost constraints together.To seed the debugging ground-truth dataset for evaluation, we mine internal engineering-support Slack threads and use an LLM to identify threads that link to an orchestrated workflow, describe a resolved problem, and match the class of issue Pensive AI handles. A second model synthesizes a reference debugging response from the relevant discussion. Paired with logs from that workflow failure, it becomes a concrete evaluation row in our evals dataset. This approach works only retrospectively, because Pensive AI in production aims to provide debugging guidance before such a Slack discussion happens.We also made the debugging generation process visible. Tracing follows the request through Pensive, with child spans for each log fetch and extraction tool call. Our tracing backend based on Braintrust brings the prompt, completion, tool calls, and latency into a single view. During early product development, that visibility helped us inspect low-performing debugging responses in context instead of guessing which input or operation caused them. Tracing helped us improve the responses and fill context gaps even before we had comprehensive evals. In production, the API and UI return the trace identifier with the response, so feedback can lead directly to the trace for in-depth analysis.Part 4: Keeping quality in the release pathEvaluation is not only for experiments with LLM orchestration, models, prompts, or context changes. Changes to log selection, trimming logic, or a source system can change what the model sees and therefore change extraction quality. We use the same evaluation harness and evaluators throughout local development and Pensive AI deployment so those effects are visible before users encounter them.For each pull request, the code branch is deployed to an isolated preview environment and a CI job runs an experiment with our evals against that isolated environment. Precision and inclusion thresholds gate the merge. The job also runs after a build is promoted, catching interactions that were not present when individual pull requests were evaluated in isolation. If the promoted build misses its thresholds, it alerts the on-call engineer to investigate or roll back.The evaluator runs on a schedule against production to surface gradual drift or external changes. Developers can also trigger evaluation experiments remotely while iterating, using the same deployed-environment path as CI. Consistent infrastructure makes the results comparable across local iteration, preview builds, promoted builds, and production.Part 5: Looking for feedback signal from usersThe system is only valuable if it reduces the amount of manual debugging and log chasing done by our users. We wanted a measurement that was available from product telemetry and close to the behavior Pensive AI was designed to change. Manual debug-log exploration became one of the main signals. The Pensive interface already offers links to logs for a failed step attempt. To estimate whether the feature reduced raw-log hunting, we compared failed step attempts where someone interacted with Pensive AI with those where no one did. The second group averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions. This observational comparison does not establish causality or a specific reduction in mean time to resolution, but it suggests that focused diagnosis often allows practitioners to inspect fewer raw logs. Programmatic MCP access also lets teams build operational flows with their terminals or custom agentic experiences around the same diagnosis service.Another more explicit signal we collect is thumbs up and thumbs down on the debugging response. These feedback signals land directly alongside the internal traces so we can quickly associate feedback to the complete log of inputs/outputs and the path the AI took to arrive at the answer. More importantly, we created an internal business-hours alerting system where each thumbs down response sends us a Slack alert. This was valuable to resolve a lot of rough edges and context gaps initially in the product and is helping us improve the product continuously even today.Figure 4. Feedback loop. A thumbs up or down joins the exact LLM trace that produced the response, by the same logId stamped during generation. Traces and feedback feed ground truth and eval datasets, and each thumbs down sends a Slack alert during business hours.Part 6: Future Work building on these foundationsPensive AI is the foundation for more work that goes beyond diagnosis and recommended remediations. We are exploring “Pensive AI Deepthink,” an opt-in managed agentic experience with higher cost and latency. It builds on the precise, low-latency analysis produced by Pensive AI Debugging and gathers additional context from internal documentation, manuals, past Slack discussions, source code, read-only warehouse queries, and Spark execution details. A routing step directs the investigation to the appropriate skill, such as Spark failures, data-audit failures, or late workflows. This keeps the shared starting point stable and deterministic while allowing the investigation to become more specialized, further improving recall. We are also in talks with the Spark team to leverage Pensive AI responses for failure debugging analysis and A/B comparison for upcoming platform migrations.We also plan to invest in “Pensive AI Error Classification”. Hard-to-maintain legacy rules also classify failures by restartability and by whether they are platform or user caused. Maestro acts on those labels and changes its retry behavior accordingly like failing fast or tuning the default number of retries (platform errors are tried more than user errors by default). Error classifications must meet a higher bar than error extractions and debugging alone. Moving the majority of the error classifications to AI would let us retire most of the remaining rule-maintenance burden and avoid retrying unknown failures that were unlikely to succeed. For restartability, the costliest error is classifying a recoverable failure as non-restartable, because Maestro will turn a step that could have been recovered into a hard failure, leading to end user alerts and manual remediations. The evaluation framework will need to be tuned around that outcome before AI-enabled classifications can take on those decisions. Equally important, we must avoid retrying non-transient failures that will not succeed, because retries waste compute and delay data pipelines.Our work on Pensive AI in Data Platform addresses concrete user pain points in debugging, improves maintainability for platform owners, and improves precision and recall for error extraction. Pensive AI extends coverage to failures that legacy Pensive previously classified as unknown. Reliability comes from the system around the AI model calls: bounded error extractions, compatible client data contracts, responsive delivery, reproducible evaluations, caching and tracing, and release controls that keep quality and cost visible as the platform changes.Part 7: AcknowledgementsThis work would not have been possible without our stunning colleagues across Data Platform and our Data Engineering and Analytics partners who provided early feedback. While we cannot name everyone individually, we are deeply grateful for their contributions, which shaped both response quality and the product experience. Special thanks to Adith Swaminathan for advising on evaluations and inference improvements and acting as a thought partner. Thank you to the Orchestration team members, especially Deepak Ramalingam and Malcolm Ramirez for their additional engineering contributions.For dogfooding and integrating Pensive AI as part of user support, we also thank the engineering support organization (ESO Team). We also thank Abhishek Kapatkar (Data Developer Experiences Team) and Emmie Dong (Data Movement Team) for their feedback to improve the Pensive AI integrations with the rest of the ecosystem. Special thanks to the AI Platform team (Kyle Ahn, Rob Mann) and Braintrust Team for helping with distributed tracing, evals infrastructure and model gateway runtime support.We also thank Kamran Masood, Ely Spears, Ronald Leung, Anjali Norwood, Prashanth Ramdas, Charles Smith, Harikrishna Menon and other leaders for their constructive feedback and support on the Pensive AI project.Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Predicting and detecting failures: How Azure strengthens reliability for mission-critical workloads
summary: Takeaway: Azure Failure Prediction and Detection (AFPD) is Microsoft Azure’s end-to-end system aiming to catch hardware failures before they interrupt a workload, not after. Across the Azure fleet, AFPD has improved the prevention of hardware-related VM interruptions by 36%. SAP workloads offer a compelling example of AFPD’s value, illustrating why preventing interruptions matters for mission-critical services. But AFPD isn’t specific to SAP: it operates across General Purpose, Specialized Compute, HPC/AI, and select Storage workloads, making SAP’s experience a window into Azure’s broader approach to reliability for mission-critical third-party services. To learn more, watch our companion video to learn how AFPD helps reduce the risk of failures disrupting your critical workloads. Reliability engineered into the platform Most conversations about cloud reliability focus on what you build: zone-redundant architectures, failover patterns, and backup strategies. Less visible, but just as consequential, is what the platform does on your behalf; before a failure ever becomes an incident you need to respond to. That’s the premise behind AFPD, which became fully operational in 2024. AFPD is an end-to-end system that uses machine learning and telemetry to predict, mitigate, and remediate hardware failures in the Azure fleet before they interrupt your workloads. For a deep dive discussion into this capability, see the companion post here. How does AFPD predict and prevent hardware failures? Historically, hardware failures on any cloud platform follow a familiar pattern: a component degrades, your workload is interrupted, an engineer investigates, and a reboot or hardware replacement follows. This is the old model Azure has spent years moving away from, one built around mission-critical escalations, supply chain constraints, and manual recovery. AFPD replaces that pattern with three coordinated phases: Predict and detect: Machine learning models and detection rules continuously monitor telemetry across the Azure fleet, node behavior, component signals, and hardware-specific indicators like Solid State Drive (SSD) health, to catch patterns that indicate an active or likely future failure. Mitigate: Once a node is flagged, the mitigation service marks it not allocatable for new workloads and, where eligible, live-migrates existing customer workloads to a healthy node with no reboot, typically just a pause of a few seconds. Live migration is available on many, but not all M-series sized virtual machines (VMs); check the feature support table for more information. Where live migration isn’t possible, a notification with a redeploy deadline and recommended action is posted to the VMs Resource Health and Scheduled Events. Remediate: The affected node is pulled from production, tagged with diagnostic detail so technicians can skip redundant troubleshooting, repaired using proactively staged spare parts, and returned to the fleet. In practice, this coordinated approach has delivered measurable gains: AFPD has increased the monthly node repair rate by 80%. The result is a system that doesn’t just react faster; in many cases, it prevents the interruption from reaching you. This approach has reduced the overall number of hardware reboots by more than 36%, and the underlying system won the Best Paper Award at the 2025 IEEE Cloud Summit for its approach to predicting, mitigating, and remediating node interruptions at scale. What SAP’s result means for other workloads Every customer benefits from fewer interruptions, but SAP workloads make the case for AFPD unusually clear. SAP systems are highly sensitive to downtime; they are often the system of record for finance, supply chain, and operations, and even brief interruptions carry outsized business impact. A platform that has the ability to predict or detect hardware issues and reduce their impact before you experience an interruption isn’t a convenience for SAP customers; it’s foundational to running SAP on Azure with confidence. That sensitivity also exposed a real gap the team was candid about: many SAP customers aren’t yet aware of the notification and automation options available to them. AFPD surfaces its findings through four consistent, customer-facing channels: Resource Health, for viewing detailed health events and recommended actions on individual VMs, including live migration eligibility and redeployment deadlines. Resource Graph Explorer, for querying health status across your fleet, including large SAP landscapes that require programmatic visibility. Event Grid, for wiring AFPD events directly into your own monitoring and automation, with Azure Functions, webhooks, or REST APIs. Scheduled Events, for receiving advance VM event notifications through IMDS, enabling configured SAP HA clusters to move resources off affected nodes. The notification content is identical across Resource Health, Resource Graph, and Event Grid, so the channel you choose is a matter of scale and integration preference, not information quality. For SAP customers running at scale, that consistency is what makes automated, hands-off resiliency actually practical. It’s tempting to read AFPD as an SAP-specific feature. It isn’t. SAP is simply where the stakes are high enough that the system’s value becomes obvious fastest. AFPD operates across Azure Compute’s General Purpose and Specialized Compute offerings, HPC/AI workloads, and select Storage scenarios, meaning the same predictive, self-healing infrastructure protecting SAP landscapes today is the same infrastructure underpinning every mission-critical third-party service hosted on Azure. That’s the broader narrative worth taking away: AFPD isn’t a tier you pay up for or something you have to configure at the infrastructure layer; it runs automatically across the fleet. It’s an active, continuously improving discipline, one where machine learning models get better at predicting failure over time, where remediation gets faster because spares are already staged, and where your first signal of a problem is often a notification that it’s already been handled. For any ISV or enterprise running a downtime intolerant workload on Azure, SAP’s experience with AFPD is a preview, not an exception. What to do next Check your own notification setup. If you’re running SAP or another mission-critical workload on Azure, confirm you’re consuming AFPD events through one of these: Resource Health (RHC): Best for looking at the health of one VM, including what happened and why. Resource Graph (ARG): Best for finding affected VMs at scale across many subscriptions in a single query. Event Grid: Best for automation, since it pushes notifications as health changes so you can react without polling. Events can be sent to a REST webhook endpoint or an Azure Functions, and onward to other services such as Logic Apps, Event Hubs, or Azure Monitor alerts. Prepare your automation for Scheduled Events: Make sure your automation can process Scheduled Events for Azure Virtual Machines, including events with a NotBefore time up to seven days in the future. Configure Pacemaker for Azure Scheduled Events: For SAP high-availability clusters, follow the guidance for configuring the Pacemaker azure-events-az resource agent leveraging the relevant guides for SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES) in Azure or RHEL in Azure. Watch the full conversation. The SAP on Azure podcast episode goes deeper into the live demo of Resource Health, Resource Graph, and Event Grid notifications than this post can cover. Go deeper technically. The IEEE paper, AFPD: System for Prediction, Mitigation and Remediation of Node Interruptions in Cloud Infrastructure (IEEE) (2025 IEEE Cloud Summit Best Paper), covers the ML models and system architecture in full detail. title: [Microsoft Azure] The Platform Behind the Next AI Breakthrough
summary: This article has been written and paid for by Microsoft. The content is not WIRED editorial content. The content does not necessarily reflect the views of WIRED, its affiliates, or owner, and does not reflect any endorsement direct or indirect of Microsoft, its affiliates, or other clients. The next frontier of AI is coming into focus as agents take on longer, more strategic work. They can write and validate code, coordinate across systems, rebalance inventory as conditions change, manage production operations, or carry a migration from plan to completion. AI is no longer supporting one step; it is executing and reshaping the process itself. New models help drive this change by expanding what AI can reason about, create, and accomplish. But the combination of advances in models and infrastructure is key to moving agents from isolated tasks to sustained, high-impact work. Realizing that potential requires silicon, compute, storage, and networking to work together so workloads run faster and more reliably at scale. Agents Are a Different Kind of Workload Cloud infrastructure has evolved before to support new kinds of applications. Even the most advanced cloud-native applications often followed predictable request-and-response paths. To deliver this at scale, cloud-native architectures turned to containers, distributed services, and dynamic scaling, to make the platform more automated and flexible. Agentic applications build on that foundation but introduce another shift: long-running work whose path and resource needs are dynamic and often unpredictable. An agent may work for hours or days, moving between reasoning, data retrieval, tool use, and code execution while preserving progress between steps. Its needs may shift throughout the task. It might require a burst of computing power for one step, fast access to large amounts of data for another, and then pause while another tool or another agent finishes its work. Supporting this ebb and flow requires the platform to evolve again—this time around how agents operate. Infrastructure Must Work as One System Every layer of infrastructure is evolving for AI. Compute must respond to the changing demand of agentic workloads. Storage must preserve progress across long-running work. And networking must move data quickly among models, tools, and business systems. But improving each layer independently is no longer enough. Agent performance depends on how well those layers are evolving and how well they all work together. More computing power will not help if the platform cannot move data quickly or maintain progress between steps. Silicon, compute, storage, and networking need to be co-designed and continuously optimized as one system. This integrated approach also changes infrastructure operations. Teams need a complete view of performance, capacity, and cost so they can find bottlenecks and improve the full workload instead of tuning one component at a time. That system-wide view helps turn infrastructure improvements into faster, more reliable, cost-effective workloads. Different Workloads, One Operational Approach That consistent operational view becomes even more important as teams choose different technologies for different workloads. A customer-facing agent may prioritize low latency, while a complex workflow may need deeper reasoning. Teams need the freedom to choose the right model, run time, silicon, and environment for each workload while balancing performance and cost. But more choice can create operational complexity because each combination may require a different approach to deployment, monitoring, and optimization. An integrated platform preserves flexibility while giving teams a consistent way to operate across models and infrastructure. Teams can choose what works best without managing every combination differently. Levi Strauss & Co. And the Value of an Integrated Platform Levi Strauss & Co. began its path to AI transformation by preparing existing business systems for the future. The company moved its data centers to Microsoft Azure, consolidated ERP platforms, modernized applications, and unified its data in a governed, real-time layer. But that was only the beginning. Levi Strauss & Co. is now building a unified “super agent” to coordinate more than 1,000 domain-specific agents. Its platform must support both the critical processes that run the business today and a new class of intelligent workloads that coordinates work across functions. The lesson is clear: A durable platform must be built for current applications and whatever AI makes possible next. Three practical tests for an agentic platform Technical leaders can begin with three questions to assess readiness for an agentic platform. First, do I have the high-performance compute, storage, and networking that models and agents need—or am I trying to run tomorrow’s applications on yesterday’s platform? Second, can I choose the right model, run time, silicon, and location for each agentic workload while balancing performance, cost, complexity, and risk? Third, can I use agents to operate the platform by moving workloads into production faster, resolving incidents before disruption, and continuously improving performance, reliability, and AI economics? Building for the next decade The next decade of AI will not be defined by a single breakthrough. Models will become even more capable, agents will take on work we have not yet imagined, and infrastructure demands will shift with them. Organizations need a durable platform that can embrace each new wave of innovation without being rebuilt whenever the frontier moves. Azure is the platform foundation for that future. Microsoft has spent years bringing some of the world’s most advanced and demanding AI solutions online at massive scale. The lessons from that work continually shape Azure silicon, compute, storage, networking, and operations—and make those capabilities available to customers. This is the opportunity of Frontier Transformation: continually turning advances across the AI stack into new ways to operate, compete, and grow. Learn more at azure.com. title: [Docker] CNCF Score project improved its security posture by joining the Docker-Sponsored Open Source Program
summary: Score, a CNCF Sandbox project, recently joined the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program to strengthen the security of its container images and release pipeline. In this post, the Score maintainers share what we adopted (Docker Hub, Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, the Docker GitHub Builder, and OIDC connections), the results we measured, and how other open source projects, within the CNCF and beyond, can apply the same practices by default. The Opportunity In September 2025, the CNCF announced a partnership with Docker to expand infrastructure support for project maintainers through the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The partnership gives CNCF projects access to Docker’s security scanning tools, container registry, and best-practice resources at no cost. This aligned closely with the discussions held at the Maintainer Summit NA 2025 in Atlanta, which centered on increasing collaboration across CNCF projects and demonstrating security best practices. The Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program supports non-commercial open source projects with Docker tooling and infrastructure. Eligible projects receive: Verified Docker-Sponsored Open Source badge Removal of rate limits for developers Access to Docker Scout for software supply chain management Insights and analytics Repository logo Improved discoverability on Docker Hub Docker Hub Before: Score publishes different container images: the CLIs of score-compose, score-k8s, score-helm and score-radius; and the sample-score-app used for demos and testing. We previously published them in the GitHub Container Registry here. After: Through the DSOS Program, we now publish these images on Docker Hub, which increases their visibility and gives the community a verified, trusted source. All the container images are now available on Docker Hub. The program also provides usage analytics that show how the community uses these images. Here is an example: Docker Scout Before: As a CNCF project, Score follows the OpenSSF best practices. In addition, the OpenSSF Scorecard GitHub Action runs continuously. This was a solid foundation, but we had no dedicated security scanning tool in place. After: The DSOS Program gave us access to Docker Scout, which we now use in our pull requests and on our container registry (Docker Hub). This gives us clear visibility into the CVEs introduced or fixed by each pull request and release. The following GitHub Actions step uses docker/scout-action on every pull request to compare the image built from the PR branch with the one built from the main branch: - name: Docker Scout Comparison between main branch and current PR branch uses: docker/scout-action@v1 with: command: compare image: local://score-compose:pr-${{ github.event.number }} to: local://score-compose:main write-comment: true github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} organization: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} Here is an example of a comment posted by this docker/scout-action step in a recent Pull Request: The comment details the comparison between the two images (before versus after): size, packages updated, added or removed, CVEs introduced and resolved, and compliance with our policies in place (run as non-root, no critical CVEs, no packages with AGPL v3 licences). The analysis goes beyond the images themselves: it also covers the Go libraries and binaries they contain. The Docker Scout console also provides a single view of CVEs, packages, base images, and policies across all of our container images, which makes it easy to see what is used where, and in which version. Docker Hardened Images When Docker made Hardened Images freely available under Apache 2.0, we saw an opportunity to simplify our security posture while staying compatible with our existing Dockerfiles and workflows, even though we were already using multi-stage builds and distroless base images. Docker Hardened Images are minimal, security-focused container base images designed to reduce inherited risk in downstream projects. They are built and maintained with security and transparency as defaults, and offer: Minimal attack surface: Only required components are included. Non-root execution: Images run as non-root by default. Supply chain security: Includes published SBOMs and SLSA Level 3 build provenance. Active maintenance: Images are patched and rebuilt as vulnerabilities are disclosed. Open standards: All images are reproducible, open source, and licensed under Apache 2.0, making them compatible with CNCF governance and distribution models. The migration was straightforward. Take the score-radius CLI, which used a golang:alpine and a distroless images and now uses dhi.io/golang and dhi.io/static images. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal: In the associated PR here, image size dropped by 0.3 MB while the number of packages stayed the same and the CVE count remained at 0. We could have stayed with Debian, but chose to move to an Alpine base image (DHI provides the two options): The same applies to the NodeJS sample-score-app, which used nodejs on top of an alpine image and now uses a dhi.io/node image. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal: In the associated PR here, 22 packages were removed (including the package manager and the shell), along with 2 CVEs: Note: We were able to present a short walkthrough of our DHI integration during the CNCF webinar held on January 23, 2026, which accompanied the Docker Hardened Images announcement for CNCF projects. Docker GitHub Builder Although not directly part of the DSOS Program, we took the opportunity to adopt the new docker/github-builder GitHub reusable workflow to release our container images. This model provides a build pipeline maintained in the Docker organization, with a version-controlled BuildKit environment, multi-platform builds distributed across runners where beneficial, and signed SLSA provenance recording both the source commit and the builder identity. The trade-off is intentional. You retain control over when the build runs and which inputs it uses, while the build implementation itself lives in the Docker-maintained workflow rather than in per-repository job steps. Before, the GitHub Actions workflow to release our container images was using this sequence of actions: docker/setup-buildx-action docker/login-action docker/build-push-action cosign sign release-container-image: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: id-token: write packages: write steps: - name: Set up Docker Buildx uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 - name: Login to Docker Hub (docker.io) uses: docker/login-action@v4 with: registry: docker.io username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_RELEASE_TOKEN }} - name: Login to GitHub Container Registry uses: docker/login-action@v4 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - name: Build and push docker image id: build-push-container uses: docker/build-push-action@v6 with: context: . platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64 push: true provenance: mode=max sbom: true tags: | ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose:${{ github.ref_name }} ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose:latest docker.io/scorespec/score-compose:${{ github.ref_name }} docker.io/scorespec/score-compose:latest build-args: | "VERSION=${{ github.ref_name }}" - name: Sign container image run: | cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose@${{ steps.build-push-container.outputs.digest }} cosign sign --yes scorespec/score-compose@${{ steps.build-push-container.outputs.digest }} After, this same workflow is now only using the reusable workflow docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml: release-container-image: uses: docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1 permissions: contents: read id-token: write packages: write with: output: image push: true platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64 sbom: true cache: true context: . set-meta-labels: true set-meta-annotations: true build-args: | "VERSION=${{ github.ref_name }}" meta-images: | ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose scorespec/score-compose meta-tags: | type=ref,event=tag latest registry-identities: | - type: dockerhub registry: docker.io username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} connection_id: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_OIDC_CONNECTION_ID }} secrets: registry-auths: | - registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} Docker GitHub Builder gives us a Docker-maintained build pipeline with signed SLSA provenance and SBOM attestations, helping consumers verify the builder identity and trace images back to their source commit. Signing uses GitHub OIDC, so we don’t need to manage long-lived signing keys. With caching enabled in our workflow, cache entries are also signed and verified before reuse, helping protect against cache poisoning. See the Docker GitHub Builder documentation for more information about its security model. The following command verifies the signature on the attestation manifest for the selected image platform: TAG=latest PLATFORM=amd64 SIGNED_DIGEST=$(crane manifest scorespec/score-compose:$TAG \ | jq -r --arg platformdigest \ "$(crane digest --platform linux/$PLATFORM scorespec/score-compose:$TAG)" \ '.manifests | select(.annotations == $platformdigest) | .digest') cosign verify \ --experimental-oci11 \ --new-bundle-format \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \ --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/docker/github-builder/\.github/workflows/build\.yml@.*$' \ scorespec/score-compose@$SIGNED_DIGEST OIDC Connections Most recently, with an update released on July 21, 2026, Docker introduced OIDC connections. This feature allows pulls and pushes to Docker Hub to use a short-lived token instead of a long-lived Organization Access Token (OAT). An OIDC connection establishes a trust relationship between Docker and a trusted third party, so you no longer need to maintain long-lived credentials. Docker exchanges short-lived tokens with the other vendor, which can grant fine-grained access to your Docker resources. Before: With docker/login-action: steps: - uses: docker/login-action@v4 with: username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_TOKEN }} Or with docker/github-builder: uses: docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1 with: ... secrets: registry-auths: | - username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_TOKEN }} After: With docker/login-action: permissions: id-token: write steps: - uses: docker/login-action@v4 # v4.5.0+ env: DOCKERHUB_OIDC_CONNECTIONID: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_OIDC_CONNECTION_ID }} with: username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} Or with docker/github-builder: uses: docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1 # v1.15.0+ permissions: id-token: write with: ... registry-identities: | - type: dockerhub registry: docker.io username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} connection_id: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_OIDC_CONNECTION_ID }} By replacing a static, long-lived token with a short-lived one and making it issued on a per-workflow basis, we removed a credential that could otherwise be stolen and misused. Wrapping Up Participating in the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program has been rewarding, and it has helped Score adopt a security-by-default foundation. Using Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, OIDC connections, and the Docker GitHub Builder has strengthened the security posture of our container images and brought broader benefits to the Score projects and repositories. If you maintain a CNCF project or any open source project, we encourage you to explore the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The security improvements were measurable, and the onboarding process was straightforward. The full implementation across the Score repositories is tracked in GitHub issue #376. Attending KubeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City? Feel free to connect with the Score maintainers during the Maintainer Summit on Sunday, Nov 8th and at the Kiosk #P-17B on Thursday, Nov 12th between 10:15am and 2pm, you will see Score in actions with the new Score Labspace! You can also meet the Docker team at booth #141 in Hall C! Note: This work was completed after I joined Docker. It was, however, an initiative we wanted to pursue as CNCF project maintainers from the moment it was announced in September 2025, both to improve our security posture and to share what we learned with the broader community. We hope this post helps you strengthen the security of your own projects.

title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Polly Generative engine, TorchNeuron for Trainium, and more (October 26, 2026)
summary: A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice. Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo. The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future. The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon). Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer. The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge. Last week’s launches Here are some launches that caught my attention this week. Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 new voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural. AWS announces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33. New ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3. Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate. Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting. Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough shows the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials. Tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality. How U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link. Upcoming AWS events Mark your calendars for these upcoming events. AWS re:Invent – AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, with more than 2,200 sessions. The session catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so now is the time to build your schedule. AWS Community Days – AWS Community Day Brasil Norte takes place in Belém on October 31, closing out the 2026 Brazilian community season. Check the hub for events near you. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!
