title: [Kubernetes] Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group
summary: We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standardCertified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions. Even so, every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support. A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from. What the working group will deliverThe charter sets out three deliverables: A specification of workload behavior for each Kubernetes minor version. A method for testing each requirement against a running workload. Upstream conformance tooling that implements those tests. The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers. The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn't yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them. However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification. The specification covers how a workload runs, and importantly not what it does. Consequently, application logic is out of scope of workload conformance. The binary won't retest anything Certified Kubernetes already covers, and it won't require a particular workload packaging format, or vendor tool like policy engine, security scanner, etc. How the work is organizedTwo Special Interest Groups (SIGs) are sponsors for the working group. SIG Architecture will own the specification and tooling through a subproject, which will be created once the first artifacts are proposed by the Working Group. SIG Apps will bring the application perspective. Whenever a requirement touches another Kubernetes SIG's area, such as node behavior or networking, the working group will initiate conversations with those SIGs as well. The working group is a forum where SIGs can get involved and shape the direction of Workload Conformance while the specification is being written. We're aiming for a stable first specification and working tests within two to three Kubernetes release cycles. Get involvedThe specification will and needs to be built from real examples, so we want to hear your experiences. If you run clusters, tell us how you assess workloads today and what broke during your last upgrade or maintenance window. If you maintain an application, tell us what it needs from the cluster and where the existing guidance left you guessing. Beyond examples, the work needs reviewers for proposed requirements and contributors to write the tests and tooling. When early versions of the tests are ready, we also want early testers to run the binary against your own workloads and tell us where the results differ between runs or environments. If a requirement touches your SIG's area, help us check its scope and the test behind it. And because the subproject will outlive the working group, we're also looking for people who want to maintain it for the long term. You can find us in #wg-workload-conformance on Kubernetes Slack (visit slack.k8s.io for an invitation) and on the mailing list. The working group meets every other Wednesday at 15:00 UTC. The Zoom link and the agenda are in the meeting notes. If you want to raise a topic, add it to the agenda. Joining the mailing list usually adds the meeting invite to your calendar. Thanks to everyone who reviewed and supported the working group proposal.

title: [Kubernetes] Why Is My Kubernetes Job Still Pending? Tracing Kueue Admission with Headlamp
summary: You submit a Kubernetes Job and wait for its Pods to appear. A minute passes. Then another. The Job is still suspended, there are no application logs, and there may not even be a Pod to inspect. In a cluster managed by Kueue, this can be completely normal. Kueue may still be deciding whether the Job can use the requested resources. The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?” The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort. This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example. Before you beginYou need a Kubernetes cluster with Kueue installed, a Headlamp installation, and the 0.1.0-alpha Kueue plugin. Your Kubernetes identity must be allowed to read the Kueue resources used in this article. The alpha release provides read-only views for Kueue v1beta2 Cohorts, ClusterQueues, LocalQueues, ResourceFlavors, and Workloads. It does not add its own create, edit, stop, resume, or delete workflows. Headlamp still provides its standard YAML and resource actions where your permissions allow them. First, separate admission from Pod schedulingKueue and the Kubernetes scheduler answer different questions. Kueue admission: Should this Workload start now, considering queue policy, quota, ResourceFlavors, admission checks, and other waiting Workloads? Pod scheduling: After the Workload is admitted and the Job resumes, which nodes can run its Pods? That boundary changes the investigation. If the Workload is not admitted, stay in the Kueue section of Headlamp. If it is admitted but its Pods are still Pending, move to Headlamp's normal Job and Pod views and inspect scheduler events. Kueue admission architecture The Headlamp-first troubleshooting pathThe quickest investigation starts with the Workload, not with a shell. Tracing a pending Job through Headlamp Step 1: Open the Workloads viewIn Headlamp, open Kueue → Workloads. Select the namespace that contains the Job, then find the Workload created for it. Kueue creates a Workload to represent the resource request and admission state of a Job. In the alpha plugin, owner references are shown as Kind/name text but are not yet clickable. The Workload name normally contains the Job name, so the namespace filter and table search are the simplest ways to locate it. Before opening the detail page, the list already gives you a useful first scan: LocalQueue priority and priority class active state admitted state completion state a readable current status such as Admitted, Finished, or Inadmissible age If there is no matching Workload, check three things before going further: the selected namespace, whether the Job was submitted to a LocalQueue, and whether your Kubernetes account can list Workloads. The plugin performs permission checks and displays an access message when the current identity cannot read a resource. Step 2: Read status, conditions, and eventsOpen the Workload. Start with its current status and conditions, not with the full YAML. For admission troubleshooting, the most important condition types are QuotaReserved and Admitted. Admitted=True means Kueue has admitted the Workload. The Job can resume, so any remaining Pending Pods belong to the scheduling branch of the investigation. QuotaReserved=False with a reason such as Pending means Kueue has not reserved quota. The condition message explains what prevented the reservation. An Inadmissible status means the Workload currently cannot fit the available queue configuration. A missing covered resource, unsuitable ResourceFlavor, stopped queue, or admission check can all lead you here. For example, a condition message may report that Kueue could not assign a ResourceFlavor because the ClusterQueue has insufficient CPU quota. That message is the first real answer to “Why is my Job still pending?” The rest of the Headlamp journey explains the configuration behind it. Also check the Events section. Conditions describe the current state; events help show what recently changed or what Kueue attempted. Step 3: Compare the Workload's request with its assignmentStay on the Workload detail page and inspect the PodSets and resource requests. The plugin shows the requested Pod count, CPU, memory, and other resources that Kueue evaluates together. This matters because a Job with parallelism: 3 and a one-CPU request per Pod asks Kueue for three CPUs in total. Looking at only one Pod's template would underestimate the Workload. If quota has already been reserved, the same page also shows the assigned ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavors, and admitted resource usage. If those admission assignments are absent, the Workload has not reached that point yet. In our example, the Workload requests: three Pods three CPUs in total 600 MiB of memory in total The next question is where that request entered Kueue. Step 4: Follow the linked LocalQueueUse the LocalQueue link on the Workload detail page. A LocalQueue is the namespace-level entry point used by the Job. It connects namespaced Workloads to a cluster-scoped ClusterQueue. The LocalQueue page shows: its namespace and connected ClusterQueue stop policy and current status pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events related Workloads in the same namespace This page answers two practical questions: Did the Job enter the queue you expected, and is it the only Workload waiting there? If the LocalQueue is inactive or stopped, that may already explain the wait. If it is active, follow the linked ClusterQueue to inspect the capacity behind it. Step 5: Inspect ClusterQueue capacity and usageA ClusterQueue represents the cluster-level quota and admission policy available to one or more LocalQueues. On its Headlamp detail page, compare the Workload request with: covered resources nominal quota for each ResourceFlavor current reservations and usage borrowing and lending limits pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts queueing strategy and stop policy preemption, fair-sharing, flavor-fungibility, and admission-check settings Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events For the example in this article, the ClusterQueue provides a nominal quota of two CPUs and two Pod slots. The Workload asks for three of each. The condition message and the ClusterQueue page now tell the same story: the Workload does not fit, so Kueue leaves the Job suspended. This is an admission-capacity problem. It is not evidence that kube-scheduler failed to find a node. Step 6: Check ResourceFlavor and Cohort when neededQuota is not always a single pool. A ResourceFlavor can represent a class of compute through node labels, taints, tolerations, or topology settings. Use the ResourceFlavor link from the ClusterQueue when the condition mentions flavor assignment or when the Workload requires a particular hardware class, such as GPU nodes. If the ClusterQueue belongs to a Cohort, follow that link too. Cohorts let ClusterQueues share unused quota. The Headlamp page shows parent and child Cohorts, member ClusterQueues, referenced ResourceFlavors, resource groups, borrowing and lending limits, and fair-sharing information. These pages help answer a more subtle question: Is the Workload blocked because the queue has no quota of its own, because it cannot borrow enough, or because no suitable flavor can be assigned? What we learned without leaving HeadlampFor the sample pending Job, the UI gives us a complete explanation: The Workload is not admitted. Its QuotaReserved condition is false and the message points to insufficient quota. The Workload requests three CPUs and three Pod slots. Its LocalQueue is active and points to the expected ClusterQueue. The ClusterQueue provides only two CPUs and two Pod slots. Kueue therefore keeps the Job suspended until quota becomes available or the queue configuration changes. The important part is not that Headlamp invents a new status. It reads the same Kubernetes API objects as other clients, then places the related resources and human-readable values in one connected investigation. If the Workload is admitted, switch viewsSuppose the Workload detail page shows Admitted=True, but the application is still not running. Kueue has completed its part of the decision. Continue in Headlamp's standard Kubernetes views: Open Workloads → Jobs and inspect the Job state and events. Open Workloads → Pods and filter by the Job name or namespace. Select a Pending Pod and read its Events section. At this stage, look for scheduler concerns such as insufficient node capacity, node affinity, taints and tolerations, topology constraints, persistent-volume binding, or image-pull failures. This handoff is the most useful troubleshooting rule in the article: Not admitted: investigate Kueue resources in Headlamp. Admitted, but Pods are Pending: investigate Job, Pod, node, and scheduler information in Headlamp. A repeatable Headlamp checklistWhen the next Job does not start, use this short path: Open Kueue → Workloads and select the correct namespace. Find the Workload associated with the Job. Check the readable status, Admitted, and QuotaReserved conditions. Read the condition message and recent events. Compare PodSet resource requests with any admission assignments. Follow the LocalQueue link and confirm its status and ClusterQueue. Follow the ClusterQueue link and compare quota, reservations, usage, and policy. Inspect ResourceFlavor or Cohort details when the message points to flavor selection or shared quota. If admitted, move to Headlamp's Job and Pod views. What Headlamp replaces during this investigationThe plugin does not replace kubectl or kueuectl for scripts, exact object output, or changes. It replaces the repetitive UI-less navigation needed during an interactive investigation. Question Headlamp path Command-line equivalent Is the Workload admitted? Kueue → Workloads → status and conditions kubectl describe workload <workload-name> -n <namespace> Which LocalQueue did it enter? Workload → linked LocalQueue kubectl get localqueue <localqueue-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml Which ClusterQueue provides quota? LocalQueue → linked ClusterQueue kubectl get clusterqueue <clusterqueue-name> -o yaml Which flavor or shared quota matters? ClusterQueue → ResourceFlavor or Cohort kubectl get resourceflavor <flavor-name> -o yaml or kubectl get cohort <cohort-name> -o yaml What happened after admission? Workloads → Jobs and Pods → events kubectl describe job <job-name> -n <namespace> or kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> For scripts and GitOps workflows, the command line remains the right tool. For a person asking “why is this waiting?”, the linked Headlamp path is usually faster to read. Optional: reproduce the pending scenarioThe plugin repository includes sample Cohort, ClusterQueue, LocalQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Job manifests for local testing. Apply those examples to a cluster where Kueue is installed, then open the Kueue section in Headlamp. To reproduce the specific quota mismatch used in this article, configure a ClusterQueue with two CPUs and two Pod slots, then submit a three-Pod Job that requests one CPU per Pod. The Job enters its LocalQueue, Kueue creates a Workload, and the Workload remains pending because the combined request is larger than the available quota. Keeping this setup separate from the main walkthrough is intentional: once the resources exist, the investigation itself should happen in Headlamp. Current alpha limitationsThe 0.1.0-alpha release is an initial read-only view of the Kueue admission path. The plugin does not add its own create, edit, pause, resume, or delete flows. Workload owner references are displayed as text and are not currently navigable. The UI depends on the Kubernetes permissions of the identity used by Headlamp. Metrics and a visual relationship map are possible follow-up areas rather than features of this release. These limits are useful to state clearly: the plugin's current purpose is to make admission state and resource relationships easier to inspect. Developed during LFX MentorshipThe plugin was developed during CNCF LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 2 using TypeScript, React, Kubernetes APIs, and Headlamp's plugin system. Utkarsh Raj implemented the plugin with guidance and review from René Dudfield (@illume) and Kevin Hannon (@kannon92). Feedback from the Headlamp and Kueue communities shaped the resource views, status presentation, navigation, documentation, tests, and first alpha release. Try it and share feedbackExplore the plugin source and README, read the 0.1.0-alpha release documentation, or share feedback in the release issue. If a pending Workload is still difficult to explain after following the Headlamp path, that is exactly the kind of feedback that can improve the plugin.

title: [Cloudflare] Introducing Spend Management: Spending limits and alerts for Cloudflare
summary: Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever.Although we’ve had usage notifications and budget alerts available to paid plans for a while, this doesn’t solve the problem completely; informing is not the same as controlling.You can now set spending thresholds and choose to have Cloudflare pause activity when those limits are reached, thus avoiding unexpected bills from unplanned usage. Today, we're introducing Spend Management in Beta, for any pay-as-you-go (PayGo) customer, starting with Workers and Durable Objects.Use Spend Management alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway already supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway.How it worksYou can start using Spend Management using the dashboard, cf CLI, or REST API.In the dashboard, head over to Manage Account > Billing > Spend limits and enable the products for which you want to control spending.When you enable controls on a product, you can define a spending limit, specify a recipient email for notifications, and set one or more alert thresholds.If you configure a recipient email, Cloudflare will send notifications when the evaluated spend reaches one of the thresholds or your spending limit. When the limit is reached, a blocking policy is enforced and your product is paused automatically.If you go to the dashboard, you can see the current billing cycle costs for each supported product in near real time (under 10 minutes), and manage your settings and thresholds from there. The overview panel tells you which products have thresholds and limits configured. In this example, you can see that Workers triggered two alerts before hitting the hard limit.Note that the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, not when you deploy a Worker or create a spending cap; a subscription starting October 10 generally has a cycle of October 10-November 10 — not a calendar month.The dashboard also shows an audit log, so you can see who changed a limit and when, or when a cap was reached.As with most Cloudflare services, Spend Management is also an API that you can use programmatically; the documentation can be found in our Developer Documentation. Here’s an example, but using the API:curl --fail-with-body --request POST \ "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID}/billing/spend-policies" \ --header "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \ --header "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }'And, of course, you can use cf, the CLI for the entire Cloudflare API:cf billing spend-policies list cf billing spend-policies create cf billing spend-policies get cf billing spend-policies update cf billing spend-policies delete cf billing spend-policies audit list cf billing spend-policies activity list cf billing spend-policies create --body '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }'Once a cap is enforced, new invocations of that product are rejected. Note that we only pause customer-code invocations that incur costs — in Workers, for example, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations are paused, but static assets continue to be served.To resume service, you can:Raise the limit above the current cycle’s accumulated spend.Disable or delete the blocking policy.Wait until the next billing cycle, when the existing block expires.That’s it. You can start using Spend Management for Workers and Durable Objects today, and other products will follow soon.Read on to learn how we built the system, and what’s going to happen next.How we built Spend ManagementAs easy and straightforward as it seems on the surface, building a system like this at Cloudflare scale was no small feat. From an invocation anywhere on our distributed network to a blocking decision that we need to apply globally, building Spend Management required working with multiple teams, changing code in existing systems, and creating new systems from scratch.Let’s start by looking at the bird's-eye view of a capped billable event:Now let's dig deeper.Collecting and aggregating close to the sourceEach invocation produces usage measurements: requests, CPU time, execution duration, or storage operations, depending on the product. But transporting and processing this volume of raw data all the way from the sources down to the rating engine would not scale or be efficient.So what we do is we collect and aggregate the measurements as close to the source as possible using a two-stage metering pipeline that combines events into usage aggregates, so the engine sees accumulated usage rather than having to process all the events one by one.Let's look at a diagram.The first stage reduces raw-event volume close to parsing down to one-minute windows. Each metering parser converts raw events into usage measurements, then combines matching measurements into typically one-minute buckets. Still, several records can describe the same account and time window.In the second stage, a separate service merges those first-stage partial aggregates using the same grouping rules, but over typically five-minute windows, and further reduces the volume before downstream processing by the Usage Engine. Here we also archive the consolidated aggregates; this gives us a durable dataset for later analytics and reconciliation.The nice thing about this two-stage pipeline is that it reduces the raw event volume early, so the downstream engines process only the aggregated usage they need to calculate spend and act on it. That’s what makes this practical at Cloudflare’s scale.Usage Engine: account-partitioned processingThe Usage Engine translates aggregated measurements into usage records, which are standardized records containing the account, usage window, metric, quantity, and relevant dimensions. In other words, it maps product-specific meters into supported usage metrics.We partition processing by account, so an account’s usage and subscription information meet in the same place. That lets us maintain its accumulated usage and apply included allowances without coordinating across pricing processors on every update.As you can see, we run different partitions in parallel, giving us a way to spread the work across accounts while keeping each account’s pricing state together. Also note that each partition keeps both a local state for fast access, and also a durable write-ahead logging (WAL) changelog on disk. This buys us:Less cross-partition coordination: each account’s usage and subscription state stay together.Consistent pricing: usage updates share the same allowance and accumulated-spend state.Parallel processing: different partitions calculate spend independently.Recoverability: durable state lets replacement processors rebuild and resume after failures, if necessary.Then, finally, the usage metrics are fed into the Rating Engine.The Rating EngineThe Rating Engine is the most important block of Spend Management; it turns usage into monetary value and it’s what’s able to answer the question: “Given what this account has consumed, its subscription, and its pricing, how much has it spent so far?”Here’s how it works.In essence, the Rating Engine brings together three things:Usage records: quantities such as requests and CPU milliseconds.Subscription information: the account’s billing period and plan changes.Pricing rules: rates, included allowances, and billing rounding.Usage data and subscriptions are independent streamsUsage and subscription updates arrive as independent streams, so we can’t assume they reach the Rating Engine in order. Furthermore, we have to be able to recover from a data processing failure or missing subscription information from, say, a failed webhook.If usage arrives before the subscription information needed to price it, we retain it as pending and revisit it when that information becomes available. This lets us tolerate temporary delays without treating unpriced usage as free.Tracking accumulated spendFinally, we calculate and track accumulated spend. The Rating Engine uses a product catalog database that defines usage metrics, including allowances, rates, and rounding rules, alongside the account’s subscription information. One million CPU milliseconds doesn’t necessarily mean an extra charge: the engine first applies the account’s included CPU allowance, then prices any excess. It prices accumulated usage rather than rounding and charging for each request independently.Once the accumulated spend is calculated, two steps follow:Policy evaluation: decide whether one or more warning or blocking thresholds have been reached.Reporting: we show estimated usage charges in the dashboard via our APIs, and we send out email alerts (via Cloudflare Email Service) if necessary.Asynchronous cap enforcementThe Rating Engine doesn’t sit in the request path or directly reject requests. Instead, the policy service sends the cap to our runtime configuration service and Quicksilver, our internal key-value store developed to enable fast global replication and low-latency access at planet scale. This propagates it to all our nodes asynchronously.Once the cap reaches Quicksilver, the runtime picks it up during its periodic refresh and starts rejecting capped invocations or operations.In other words, enforcement uses local state, so requests never have to wait on the Rating Engine. By reusing our existing runtime account-limit architecture, we keep rating out of the request path while distributing caps across the global network.What’s nextAny pay-as-you-go customer can start using Spend Management today. While this is a major milestone in our roadmap, it’s also just the start. Let us share some of our plans for the next few weeks and months ahead.More productsWe are starting with caps for Workers and Durable Objects, but you’ll be able to measure and cap many other Cloudflare products and primitives in the near future. We’ve built the system in a way that makes it easy and familiar for our products to onboard, so expect the catalog to grow.Closer to real timeWhile near real time under 10 minutes is a great benchmark, we’re not satisfied with it, and being the stubborn engineers we are, we have pretty good ideas on how to reduce that time even further. Expect us to shorten the gap between measurement and enforcement over time, hopefully to under a minute.Agent and application-based budgetsRight now, we measure spend by products and primitives, but there are other useful dimensions to explore when controlling costs. For example, a developer might want to monitor the costs of a specific application — such as a Worker script that uses other primitives like R2 or Workers AI. How can we measure the aggregated cost of an entire application and pause that application, rather than disabling the underlying primitives across all customer applications?Another compelling use case for cost controls is AI agents. We’ve all read horror stories about rogue agents entering unconstrained recursive reasoning loops to brute-force a problem — generating thousands of dollars in costs from high-frequency, expensive API calls, not to mention causing denial-of-service (DoS) issues on databases and other services. AI Gateway already lets you give an agent a budget for AI requests routed through it. A task can also consume compute, database, and storage resources. We want to make it possible to budget for that broader resource use across products.You’ll be able to tag the calls from your agents and our pipeline will carry that metadata from the runtime through to the Rating Engine. That will let us attribute spend and pause an application or an agentic task across products, without interrupting other unrelated applications.Get startedThis launch is a first step toward making spend controls a normal part of building on Cloudflare, alongside deploying code and monitoring your applications.Check out the billing developer documentation for more information. Start using Spend Management and tell us what works, what’s missing, or where more granular budgets would help.Join us on Discord or our socials. We’re listening!

title: Trying to understand how security tooling fits into CI/CD, for a uni case study. Would love your take!
